subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage: Note from the class teacher. Gargi came to me at the end of Monday, hands twisted together. She had tried to make up with Raghav at the water tank, but within a minute both were shouting again. "We can't fix it alone," she said. "Will you help?" I asked them to come in after school. I sat between them and set one rule: each of us speaks while the others listen. Raghav went first, fast and angry. Then Gargi told her side. By the end Raghav was staring at the floor, and Gargi's shoulders had dropped. They left together, still awkward, but talking.

qa.q: Where did Gargi and Raghav's first attempt end in shouting?
qa.a: Their first attempt ended in shouting at the water tank.

qa.q: What did Gargi realise after the shouting, and how might Gargi have felt?
qa.a: Gargi realised they could not fix it alone; twisted hands suggest Gargi felt worried and a little ashamed of the shouting.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gargi try if the talk with the teacher still stays tense, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could write down what matters most to say, or wait a few days before trying again with calmer feelings. Both could work because they slow the anger.

qa.q: How might Raghav see the talk with the teacher?
qa.a: Raghav went first and fast, then stared at the floor while Gargi spoke, so Raghav may have felt defensive and then thoughtful once listening.

grounding: Her first attempt to make up ends in shouting, so she notices they cannot fix it alone and asks the class teacher to help them take turns speaking.

subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage:
Wednesday
Tried to make up with Devika today. Didn't work. I said, 'Can we talk?' and she said, 'About how you told everyone my marks?' and I said, 'I didn't tell everyone!' and then we were both shouting again, right in the corridor. I went home and cried. Tonight I thought hard. Every time we try, it turns into the same fight. We can't fix this by ourselves. So tomorrow I'm going to ask Mrs Fernandes to sit with us.
Thursday (adding this)
She did! In the empty staff room. She said, 'Devika first, then Ayesha. No interrupting, girls.' It felt strange, but for the first time I actually heard what Devika was upset about.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Fernandes sit with them?
How did Ayesha feel after the first attempt?
qa.a: Ayesha felt upset and hopeless, crying at home after it turned into shouting again.

qa.q: What made the second try work better than the first?
qa.a: Mrs Fernandes set turns with no interrupting, so each girl could be heard instead of both shouting.

qa.q: How might Devika have experienced the talk in the staff room?
qa.a: Speaking first without being interrupted, Devika could finally explain what upset her, which may have helped her feel heard.

grounding: Shows a girl whose first try to make up ends in shouting, who sees they can't fix it alone and asks the class teacher to let each speak in turn.

subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage: Neelam and Sarita had shared a bench at the panchayat school since Class 1. Now they weren't speaking, all because of a torn library book each blamed on the other. On Monday Neelam tried: she walked up to Sarita at the hand pump and said, 'Let's forget it.' Sarita said, 'You mean forget that you tore it?' Within a minute they were shouting, and a crowd gathered. That evening Neelam sat on the roof thinking. We're only going round and round. We need someone in the middle. On Tuesday she went to Kamla Bahenji, the class teacher. At lunch Bahenji sat with both of them under the peepal tree and said, 'Sarita speaks, then Neelam. Nobody cuts in.'

qa.q: What did each girl blame on the other?
What was Neelam thinking and feeling on the roof?
qa.a: She felt frustrated that they were 'only going round and round', and saw that they needed someone in the middle.

qa.q: Why did asking Kamla Bahenji help where Neelam's first try failed?
qa.a: The teacher gave each girl a turn with no cutting in, so the talk couldn't turn into shouting at the hand pump again.

qa.q: How might Sarita see sitting under the peepal tree with the teacher?
qa.a: Sarita gets to speak first without Neelam cutting in, so she may feel respected and more willing to listen.

grounding: Illustrates a girl whose first attempt to make up ends in shouting, realising they need help, and asking the class teacher to let each speak in turn.
